title: Rennyo's letters
hookLine: the later teacher who spread Shin Buddhism through simple letters to followers

cards: Evening in a farming village in Japan, long ago. The work is done, and neighbors crowd into one house. Someone unfolds a sheet of paper and reads it aloud, slowly, so the people at the back can hear.

It isn't a learned treatise full of Chinese characters that only monks can follow. It's written in plain Japanese, in the simple script ordinary people could read, and it says the important thing in a few lines.
When the reading ends, the room says the name together. The letter came from a teacher named Rennyo.

teach.h: A LATER HEAD OF THE HONGANJI.
teach.b: First, who he was. Rennyo came generations after Shinran, a descendant who became head of the Honganji, the temple that grew from Shinran's grave.
Tradition remembers him as the teacher who carried Shin Buddhism out of a small circle and into villages across Japan. Second, his tool: the letter.

Rennyo wrote to followers in plain Japanese, in the simple script, not the dense Chinese of scholars. Tradition says his letters were copied by hand, carried from village to village, and read aloud in gatherings.
Shin Buddhists still read them in services; one branch calls them Ofumi, the letters, and another Gobunsho. Third, what the letters keep saying.

teach.h: ENTRUST, THEN SAY THE NAME IN THANKS.
teach.b: Again and again they return to a short core: entrust yourself to Amida with a single heart, let go of trying to earn your way, then say the name in thanks. He didn't add new layers. He kept taking layers off.
Fourth, the letter people know best, often called the letter on white ashes.
It says, in effect: in the morning we may have rosy cheeks, and by evening be white ashes. Life is that short and that uncertain, so don't put off the one thing that matters.
It is read aloud at Shin funerals. Rennyo's gift was not a new idea. It was plainness: the deep thing said in words a tired farmer could hear after dark, and remember the next morning.

how: In Jodo Shinshu temples, Rennyo's letters (called Ofumi or Gobunsho, depending on the branch) are read aloud in services, and the letter on white ashes is read at funerals.

games.q: you're Rennyo. you want Shinran's teaching to reach farmers who can't read the scholars' Chinese. what do you write?

practice: Choose one person who might need to hear from you, and compose a letter to them in your head, in as few words as you can: who it's to, the one thing you want them to know, your name. No explaining, no extra layers.
Say it over until it's plain enough to read aloud in a dim room.
